answers.Q1:
The core of this text is actually quite organized, which points away from a severe executive function deficit.
Look at ⟦h1⟧; the writer sets a specific time limit ('two hours') and tracks the deviation ('most of the evening').
That is self-monitoring, not a failure to perceive time.
⟦h2⟧ is the key to reading the procrastination correctly: they didn't open the doc because they prioritized household tasks ('dishes and the bins').
This suggests a value-based prioritization issue or avoidance, not an inability to start.
I see a lot of clients who claim they 'can't start' because their brain is foggy; this writer explicitly states *why* they didn't start.
It's a rational, albeit inefficient, sequence.
⟦h3⟧ is a strong 'away' marker.
They have identified the cause of their poor sleep (noise, new bed) and the duration (two months).
A client with ADHD often describes sleep problems as chronic and unexplained or linked to hyperarousal, but here it's clearly situational.
⟦h4⟧ is a typical 'open loop' thought.
It's minor, not a critical work failure.
Finally, ⟦h5⟧ shows a metacognitive check.
The writer acknowledges the digression ('lift... shopping') and explicitly dismisses its relevance ('nothing to do with anything').
That self-correction is a strong indicator of intact executive control.
The narrative structure is linear, chronological, and self-correcting.
It reads like a stressed, tired person, not a dysregulated one.
answers.Q2:
The procrastination in ⟦h1⟧ and ⟦h2⟧ is the most likely candidate for misinterpretation.
It looks like avoidance, which can be a symptom of anxiety or low mood (depressive inertia).
The distinction is in the *capacity* to complete.
This writer finished the chart pack by 8 AM (mentioned later: 'sent the chart pack to Marcus... replied with a thumbs up').
That shows they can execute under pressure.
The delay was a choice to do chores first, possibly to avoid the cognitive load of the commentary.
This is common in burnout or high-stress periods, not necessarily ADHD.
The poor sleep in ⟦h3⟧ is clearly environmental.
If I saw 'can't sleep' with no cause, I'd flag it.
Here, the cause is stated.
The 'legs hurt' in ⟦h5⟧ is a somatic complaint that might be dismissed, but in context, it's just a detail.
It doesn't point to a trait, just a physical state.
The main differential is ordinary stress/procrastination vs. ADHD.
The self-awareness ('I told myself...') Strongly favors the former.
answers.Q3:
I'd want to know if this pattern is new.
The text mentions 'since we moved flats two months ago'.
Is the work delay also new?
If this person has always managed work but is now struggling, it's likely situational stress or burnout.
I'd ask: 'Does this level of delay happen every week, or is this a one-off bad week?' I'd also look at the 'fridge shelf' item in ⟦h4⟧.
Is that a recurring type of minor oversight, or a one-time note?
One data point isn't enough.
I'd want a second sample from a low-stress day to see if the self-monitoring (like in ⟦h1⟧) holds up when they aren't tired.
Also, the 'thumbs up' from Marcus suggests the work product was acceptable.
If the quality is consistently good despite the time pressure, that argues against a core executive dysfunction.
answers.Q5:
A junior clinician might latch onto the procrastination in ⟦h1⟧ and the 'can't finish' vibe and jump to an ADHD diagnosis because it fits the 'time blindness' stereotype.
They might miss the explicit self-monitoring ('told myself two hours') and the rational reason for the delay (chores).
They might also over-read the poor sleep in ⟦h3⟧ as a symptom of hyperarousal, missing the clear environmental cause (noise/new bed).
Conversely, they might under-interpret the strong self-correction in ⟦h5⟧.
They might see the digression as a sign of disorganization, missing that the writer *notices* and *corrects* the digression.
The text is actually quite coherent and self-regulating.
The risk is pathologizing ordinary stress and fatigue.

answers.Q1:
The most striking part is the pattern of initiation failure mixed with successful execution when the barrier is low.
⟦h1⟧ is a classic 'lost in the task' moment.
She didn't forget the table; she went to get it, got distracted by a mundane physical action (cleaning the mug), and lost the thread of the cognitive task.
That specific type of attentional lapse—where the goal is clear, but the immediate next step disappears—is more suggestive of executive dysfunction than simple laziness.
Similarly, ⟦h2⟧ shows a very similar loop: the goal (ask about bins) is replaced by a competing impulse (food), and the original goal is dropped.
It's not that she can't do the work; it's that she can't *sustain* the specific intent when something else competes for attention.
On the other hand, ⟦h3⟧ is strong evidence *away* from a pure deficit model. She has metacognition.
She knows she needs structure, she knows the phone is a threat, and she has set up a 'body doubling' or environment control strategy.
That level of self-regulation and planning is often harder for people with severe ADHD than the distraction itself.
⟦h4⟧ is interesting because it shows insight and a somewhat detached, almost academic way of framing her own distress.
She calls it 'arithmetic,' which suggests she is monitoring her progress against a deadline objectively.
This is a cognitive style that can coexist with ADHD, but it also suggests she is not in a state of total chaos; she is calculating.
⟦h5⟧ is just a stress marker.
The 'I know' is a bit self-deprecating, but four coffees in a day, while not ideal, is a very common coping mechanism for deadline pressure, especially in academia.
It doesn't strongly point to ADHD, nor away from it; it's just context.
answers.Q2:
Honestly, this reads very much like high-functioning anxiety or simply a bad week.
The 'lost time' in ⟦h1⟧ could easily be a moment of mental fatigue or dissociation from stress.
The coffee in ⟦h5⟧ points strongly to anxiety or sleep debt.
The fact that she did 600 words in one go on Monday (⟦h3⟧ context) suggests she *can* focus deeply when motivated or in the right environment (library vs. home).
This 'bimodal' performance—great in one setting, struggling in another—is often situational rather than neurodevelopmental.
The distinction is hard to make without knowing if this is her baseline.
If she does this every week, it's a trait.
If this is just the week before a stats exam and a deadline, it's likely acute stress.
The 'clean mug' detail is specific enough to be a real memory, but it could also be a sign of a mental 'reset' when overwhelmed, which is common in burnout.
answers.Q3:
I'd want to know about her history.
Does she do this when the stakes are low?
If she's only this scattered when there's a deadline and an exam, that's performance anxiety.
If she's also losing keys, forgetting to reply to texts from friends, or having trouble starting homework when there's no deadline, that's more suggestive.
Also, I'd want to see a sample of her writing on a non-stressful topic.
The current text is very structured and self-aware, which might be a 'good day' or a 'performing normal' day.
I'd also ask about her sleep.
The coffee and the 'clean mug' distraction could just be exhaustion.
And I'd want to know if she has tried these strategies before (the 50-min blocks) and if they usually work, or if this is a new experiment.
answers.Q5:
A less experienced clinician might latch onto the 'lost time' and the coffee and call it ADHD immediately.
They might miss the strong planning in ⟦h3⟧ and the clear insight in ⟦h4⟧.
They might under-interpret the situational stress.
The 'I know' in ⟦h5⟧ might be read as a lack of impulse control, but it's more likely self-monitoring.
The bigger risk is over-pathologizing a normal, albeit stressful, academic workload.
The text is actually quite competent and self-reflective, which is often a sign of high functioning and good coping, not a lack of control.

answers.Q1:
The core issue here is procedural failure, not cognitive style.
⟦h1⟧ is a classic handover gap; she admits the cause ('local file') and the consequence, but doesn't show disorganization in *how* she processed it.
She identified the error, stated the reason, and moved on.
That's competent problem-solving, not executive dysfunction.
⟦h2⟧ shows poor time management, but again, she self-corrected by acknowledging the rush.
It's a mistake, not a pattern of inattention.
The only thing that hints at something else is ⟦h3⟧.
'Keep going over in my head' suggests rumination or anxiety about social standing rather than ADHD impulsivity.
She's not acting on the thought; she's worrying about it.
Finally, ⟦h4⟧ is a very organized, socially aware closing.
A person with significant ADHD traits in a professional context often struggles with this kind of meta-commentary on their own communication length. She's self-monitoring.
The text is structured, apologetic, and causal.
It reads like a conscientious person who made a human error under time pressure, not a neurodivergent profile.
answers.Q2:
The 'going over in my head' part ⟦h3⟧ leans more toward anxiety or high sensitivity to criticism than ADHD.
ADHD is usually about the *action* (sending the email, missing the deadline) or the *forgetting*.
This is about the *aftermath* and social interpretation.
Low mood or burnout could explain the rushed proofing ⟦h2⟧, but the self-awareness of the time slip suggests it's situational stress, not chronic low energy.
Ordinary procrastination is possible if she waited until the last minute, but the text says she 'allowed an hour,' implying she planned, just underestimated.
It's more likely a calibration error than a failure to initiate.
answers.Q3:
I’d want to see the email from Priya.
If it was passive-aggressive, her rumination is a normal reaction to conflict.
If it was neutral, it suggests an internal anxiety loop.
I’d also ask if this 'rushed proofing' is a one-off due to Dana’s departure or a chronic pattern where she consistently underestimates task duration.
A single week of transition chaos explains a lot of the 'messiness.'
answers.Q5:
A junior clinician might latch onto 'working from the old shared version' as evidence of disorganization or failure to update.
They might miss that she explicitly identified the *technical* cause (local file vs. shared drive).
They might over-read the 'going over in my head' as a symptom of ADHD inattention (mind wandering) rather than anxiety (worry).
They might also miss the strong organizational markers in the apology and the causal explanations.
They’d likely rate this higher than it deserves because they’re looking for 'messy' and finding 'explanatory.'

answers.Q1:
The text is a classic 'executive dysfunction under load' narrative rather than a pure attentional deficit.
⟦h1⟧ and ⟦h3⟧ are the key markers here.
The phrasing "I'll do them soon" and "I keep saying I'll sit down... after tea" is a temporal displacement of a necessary task.
It's not that he can't do the invoices; it's that the transition from 'physical labor' to 'administrative detail' is the bottleneck.
This is very common in adults who have high competence in their trade but struggle with the 'invisible' work of business management.
The time gap in ⟦h2⟧ (five weeks) is significant because invoices are a hard constraint (cash flow), not a soft preference like reading a book.
The fact that he *knows* they are sitting there and feels the weight of it ("I'm fed up") suggests intact self-monitoring but poor initiation/execution.
This is a strong 'toward' signal for adult ADHD traits, specifically the procrastination/organization cluster.
However, ⟦h4⟧ is crucial context: he *can* perform when the task is concrete, immediate, and externally rewarded (card on the spot).
This suggests the issue isn't a global inability to focus or work, but a specific regulatory failure regarding delayed, internal, or administrative tasks.
⟦h5⟧ provides the physiological context: he is exhausted.
Fatigue lowers the threshold for executive function, so this might be a 'tired brain' effect rather than a neurodevelopmental one, though the pattern of 'I know I should, I just don't do it' persists even when he is presumably less tired on Sundays.
answers.Q2:
The primary alternative is burnout or severe burnout-adjacent depression.
When you are working 12-hour days (⟦h5⟧), the brain conserves energy by shutting down non-essential functions.
Invoice processing is 'non-essential' in the moment of survival.
The 'after tea' procrastination (⟦h3⟧) is a very common coping mechanism for high-stress professionals who feel no slack in their schedule.
A person with low mood might also show this 'inertia,' but the writer here is active, complaining, and seeking solutions (apps).
The distinction is usually in the *duration* and the *baseline*.
If this has been his pattern for five years, it's ADHD.
If this is the third month of this intense workload, it's likely stress-induced executive dysfunction.
Anxiety is less likely to be the primary driver here because the tone is frustration with self, not fear of the task.
He isn't afraid of the invoices; he's just not doing them.
That's more consistent with ADHD or fatigue than anxiety.
answers.Q3:
I need to know the baseline.
Is he always like this with admin, or is this new since spring?
If he used to do invoices on Tuesdays, and now he can't, that's a change in function, likely due to load/mood.
If he has always been the 'I'll do it Sunday' guy, that's trait.
I also need to know about his sleep.
"Shattered" is doing a lot of work there.
If he's sleeping 4 hours, I'm discounting the ADHD hypothesis significantly.
Finally, I'd want to see if he has other domains affected.
Does he lose tools?
Does he forget appointments?
The invoice issue is isolated to business admin in this text.
If it's only invoicing, it's a workflow problem, not a neurodevelopmental one.
If he also forgets to eat or loses his van keys, it's broader.
answers.Q5:
A less experienced clinician might see "I'm fed up" and "shattered" and jump straight to depression or burnout, missing the specific pattern of executive failure.
Or, conversely, they might see "I can do it when I know the job" and conclude he's just lazy or disorganized, missing the nuance that he *can* organize when the stakes are immediate and concrete.
The risk is over-pathologizing a tired tradesman or under-pathologizing a person with adult ADHD who is masking well in his trade but failing in his business.
They might also miss the specific 'initiation' deficit (starting the task) vs. the 'completion' deficit, which are treated differently.

answers.Q1:
The core of this is the initiation gap in ⟦h1⟧.
It's not that she couldn't do it; she 'knew exactly what to do.' That is a classic executive function snag—the engine is there, but the ignition is sticky.
I see this a lot in young adults who have coasted on intelligence or support in university and then hit a wall at work.
The specific detail 'sat open on my screen' is telling; it suggests the task was visible but ignored, which is more about attentional regulation or anxiety paralysis than simple memory loss.
Then there is ⟦h2⟧, the 'stockroom' incident.
This is a bit more ambiguous.
Forgetting the purpose of a trip is a very common, low-level working memory slip.
In isolation, it's nothing.
But paired with the spreadsheet, it starts to look like a pattern of 'input' (I need to go in / I need to send this) getting lost before 'output' (actually going / actually sending).
On the other hand, ⟦h3⟧ and ⟦h4⟧ are strong counter-evidence, or at least context.
She was 'early every day' and finished modules early.
That shows she *can* regulate when the structure is high and the novelty is fresh.
The fact that she bought a planner (⟦h5⟧) and it 'has helped' is also a point away from a severe neurodevelopmental deficit; she is actively compensating, and it's working.
The apology-heavy tone and the request for off-hours (⟦h6⟧) suggest high anxiety or shame, which can mimic or exacerbate ADHD symptoms, but it's not proof of the disorder itself.
It's a very 'normal' struggling-with-adulthood letter.
answers.Q2:
Honestly, most of this is anxiety or just bad sleep.
The 'sat open on screen' thing?
Could be she was terrified of making a mistake in the spreadsheet and her brain froze.
That’s performance anxiety, not necessarily ADHD. The stockroom thing?
Could be she was distracted by a thought, or just tired.
If she’s sleeping 5 hours a night, everything looks like ADHD.
I’d want to know if she’s been sleeping.
Also, low mood can look exactly like this—lack of initiation, forgetfulness, feeling like things are hard.
If she’s depressed, the 'I knew what to do but didn't do it' is anhedonia/psychomotor retardation, not executive dysfunction.
The distinction is: does she have this in low-stakes situations too?
Or only when she’s judged?
The text feels very 'judged'—manager, work, 'trying hard not to get things wrong.' That leans toward anxiety.
answers.Q3:
I need to know if this is new.
Has she always had trouble starting tasks, or is this just because it’s her first 'real' job?
I’d ask for a specific example from university.
Did she finish essays on time?
If she always used the last minute and got an A, that’s a different profile than someone who always struggled.
I also need to ask about her sleep hygiene directly.
And I’d want to see the 'planner'—is it a complex system she maintains, or a blank notebook she stares at?
The text says it 'has helped,' but I’d want to verify if she’s actually writing things down or just having the object as a talisman.
Also, the 'earlier message' she refers to—what was that?
If she’s been emailing back and forth, the tone might shift.
But mostly, I need a day in the life.
Does she forget to eat?
Does she lose keys?
Or is it just work-specific?
If it’s just work, it’s likely job anxiety or a bad fit, not a disorder.
answers.Q5:
A junior clinician might latch onto ⟦h1⟧ and ⟦h2⟧ and say, 'Classic ADHD, give her a stimulant.' They might miss the context of ⟦h3⟧—that she was actually doing well for the first week.
They might miss that she is *using* a tool (⟦h5⟧) and it's working.
They might pathologize the anxiety.
Or they might dismiss it entirely as 'just stress' and fail to ask about the underlying executive function gaps that are now exposed by the new environment.
The risk is either over-diagnosing a normal adjustment period or under-diagnosing a real struggle that needs support strategies, not just 'calm down.'

The text describes a single incident rather than a pattern, but the style is telling.
⟦h1⟧ represents the most 'ADHD-like' moment: the action precedes the interaction.

It is not just that he snapped; it is that his hands moved before his mouth finished.
That said, ⟦h5⟧ provides crucial context.

That is a communication failure common in high-stress retail, not necessarily an attention deficit.
He forgot to *say* it, not that he forgot the *task* existed.
⟦h3⟧ serves as a strong counter-point.
He managed the till, the rota, and the delivery.
That demonstrates executive function working well.
If he had a pervasive working memory issue, the 'penny' precision suggests he is either very organized or hyper-focused.
⟦h2⟧ provides a massive alternative explanation.

The wording 'Not sure. Text, probably.' in ⟦h4⟧ shows decision paralysis, which could be ADHD, but it is also just being tired at the end of a shift.
answers.Q2:
⟦h1⟧ could be pure anger management failure due to stress.
⟦h2⟧ is the biggest confounder: depression, grief, or burnout look exactly like this.

⟦h4⟧ could be simple fatigue.

answers.Q3:

answers.Q5:

answers.Q1:
The first thing that catches my eye is ⟦h1⟧.
The image of sharpening the pencil twice before starting is very specific.
It could be a ritual, which we see a lot in anxiety or OCD, but it sits right next to the 'most of the evening' delay.
That combination—high arousal/ritual before the task, then the long stretch of time—is often a proxy for executive dysfunction in my practice, though here it's filtered through Mum's memory, so I'm wary. Then there's ⟦h2⟧.
This is the most clinically relevant sentence.
The conditionality ('when I knew what was expected') is a classic marker.
It suggests the writer isn't lacking ability or motivation, but struggles with the transition from expectation to action, or maintaining engagement once the structure is removed.
It's a very 'ADHD-like' dependency on external scaffolding.
Finally, ⟦h3⟧ points toward a persistent trait.
'Every year' rules out a one-off stressor.
'Untidy and rushed' suggests a speed-accuracy trade-off, common in people who lose the thread of detail while moving fast, or simply who have poor motor control or low tolerance for the effort of neatness.
It's a weak signal on its own, but consistent with the other two.
I'm treating ⟦h4⟧ as neutral; it's just the writer correcting the record, showing they are reflective and distinct from their parents' narratives, which is actually a good sign of self-awareness, not a trait itself.
answers.Q2:
Honestly, most of this could be low self-esteem or anxiety.
The 'sharpening' could be a compulsion to 'prepare' to avoid the fear of failure.
The conditional teaching comment could just be a strict teacher and a student who needed clear instructions, which is normal for a child.
The handwriting could just be... bad handwriting. What distinguishes them? Context and pervasiveness.
If the writer is currently struggling with similar tasks in work or relationships, or if they had to use compensatory strategies (like the volcano being planned early to avoid the chaos of last-minute panic), it leans toward ADHD.
If they were generally disorganized but high-achieving in other areas, it’s less clear.
Also, the 'rushed' handwriting might just be a physical habit, unrelated to attention.
answers.Q3:
I’d want to know if the writer is currently functional.
Do they still struggle with starting tasks?
Do they have a history of compensatory successes (like the volcano ribbon) that mask the effort involved?
I’d also ask about the 'long way home' story—is that a genuine memory of getting distracted, or another 'Mum story' that might be exaggerated?
I’d want a sample of their current writing to see if the 'untidy' trait persists, and ask about their relationship with time: do they consistently misjudge duration?
answers.Q5:
A junior clinician might latch onto the 'pencil sharpening' and call it a ritual, missing the executive function piece.
Or they might see the 'conditional' teaching comment and immediately diagnose ADHD, ignoring that many kids are just reactive to authority.
They might also miss that the writer is actively distancing themselves from their parents' narratives, which is a sign of healthy ego differentiation, not a symptom.

The 'usual history' regarding childhood symptoms is missing, but I'd ask about current functional impairment first.
answers.Q5:
A junior might latch onto ⟦h1⟧ and the 'I don't remember' in ⟦h3⟧ and diagnose based on the talkativeness.
They might miss ⟦h5⟧ which shows good planning.
They might also over-read the minor inconsistency in the fish count (implied) as disorganization, when it's just a casual recount.
They might underestimate the coherence of the narrative, which is actually quite strong.

Dennis caught three roach and mentioned it often

There are eleven, or twelve, I'd have to count

confounders.alternative_explanation: Poor sleep after a recent move to a louder flat could explain tiredness and slower starts.
confounders.quote: Still sleeping badly since we moved flats two months ago

planted_cues.quote: I told myself two hours for the commentary section and it has now been most of the evening
I only opened the document at nine because I did the dishes and the bins first

design.purpose: a quarterly report due on Friday (traits: task_initiation: moderate; time_estimation: weak)

vignettes.text: Thursday night and the quarterly report is due tomorrow at five, which is fine, because the numbers from claims came in on Tuesday and I had already pulled the loss ratios into the template by Wednesday lunch, and then Priya asked me to check her reserve figures too, and that took the whole afternoon, and the lift in our building was out so I carried the shopping up four floors, which has nothing to do with anything but my legs hurt. Anyway the report. I told myself two hours for the commentary section and it has now been most of the evening, I only opened the document at nine because I did the dishes and the bins first. Still sleeping badly since we moved flats two months ago, the street is louder than the old one and the bed is a different bed, so I was up at five anyway and sent the chart pack to Marcus before work, and he replied with a thumbs up by eight. That part went well. The commentary I think I can finish by eleven, maybe midnight, then read through it once in the morning. Need to remember to ask Dan about the fridge shelf.

confounders.alternative_explanation: High caffeine intake can cause restlessness and scattered focus.
confounders.quote: I have had four coffees today

confounders.alternative_explanation: Exam anxiety could explain difficulty concentrating on writing.
confounders.quote: I am quite nervous about it

planted_cues.quote: went to find the table from the second survey, and came back ten minutes later with a clean mug and no table
went to the kitchen to ask my flatmate about the bins and came back with a toastie and still no answer about the bins

design.purpose: a thesis chapter that is not getting written (traits: distractibility: moderate; working_memory: weak)

vignettes.text:
Chapter three is at 1,100 words. It goes to my supervisor on the 20th and today is the 11th. I would call this a tragedy but it is mostly arithmetic.

On Monday I wrote 600 of those words in one go at the library, because the kitchen at home was empty and nobody was cooking. That went fine. On Tuesday I opened the file, went to find the table from the second survey, and came back ten minutes later with a clean mug and no table.

I have had four coffees today. I know. The stats exam is on Thursday as well and I am quite nervous about it.

I did send the method section on time last week, so at least one person at the university has proof I exist. My supervisor wrote back with three comments, all fair, and I fixed them the same evening.

Today I made a plan of two blocks of 50 minutes with my phone in my bag. Block one happened. Then I went to the kitchen to ask my flatmate about the bins and came back with a toastie and still no answer about the bins. Block two is after dinner.

confounders.alternative_explanation: Ruminating about a conflict with a colleague, which could explain distraction and the rushed proofing.
confounders.quote: a message that I keep going over in my head

confounders.alternative_explanation: An ordinary process failure: the colleague saved the calendar locally and did not mention it.
confounders.quote: she'd saved it as a local file and nobody told me

design.knowledge_target: Telling goal-loss digression that eventually resolves from anxious rumination that circles one worry, in free adult text (textual markers, not diagnostic criteria).

planted_cues.quote: Anyway, my sister has the same problem with her boiler manual
I'd allowed an hour to check the proofs and it took nearer three

design.purpose: explaining why last week's project handover went wrong (traits: discourse_tangentiality: moderate; time_estimation: weak)

vignettes.text: Hi Jo, you asked how the handover went and I said fine, which was not true. Here is what happened. Dana moved to the events team on Friday, so on Thursday I was meant to take over her campaign calendar and the supplier logins. The logins worked, because I asked IT on Monday and they sorted it the same day. The calendar did not, because she'd saved it as a local file and nobody told me, so for two days I was working from the old shared version. That's the ordinary reason, really. Anyway, my sister has the same problem with her boiler manual, it's a PDF on a laptop she has since sold, and her whole building spent a weekend... sorry. The newsletter went out on Tuesday with the wrong date for the webinar. I'd allowed an hour to check the proofs and it took nearer three, so the last two pages got a quick look. Priya in design also copied me on a message that I keep going over in my head, the one about 'ownership', but that's another email. So it was a local file, a wrong date and rushed proofing. I'm sorry this ran so long.

confounders.alternative_explanation: Higher workload and long tired days could explain late invoices and overrunning jobs.
confounders.quote: Business has got busier since spring, I'm on site by seven most days and not home till gone seven, and by then I'm shattered

confounders.alternative_explanation: Unexpected site conditions in an old house are an ordinary reason for a job overrunning.
confounders.quote: the plaster being thicker than it looked and the old cable run under the floor not where the drawings said

design.knowledge_target: Reading time language (vague quantifiers, 'just' tasks, retrospective underestimation) as evidence of time-estimation difficulty versus workload or avoidance.

planted_cues.quote: I said about two and a half days and it took four
I keep saying I'll sit down with them after tea

design.purpose: why jobs keep overrunning and invoices go out late (traits: time_estimation: strong; task_initiation: weak)

vignettes.text: Same story every month and I'm fed up with it. A job I quote at about two days ends up three. Last week it was a rewire in a 1960s semi, I said about two and a half days and it took four, though a fair bit of that was the plaster being thicker than it looked and the old cable run under the floor not where the drawings said. That's the house, not me. The week before I did a consumer unit swap in one morning, exactly as quoted, customer was pleased and paid by card on the spot. So I can do it when I know the job. Business has got busier since spring, I'm on site by seven most days and not home till gone seven, and by then I'm shattered. Invoices wait. I'll do them soon, usually Sunday. Right now there are six sitting in a folder, the oldest about five weeks, and I keep saying I'll sit down with them after tea. One of them I did start, got as far as the customer's address. Anyone else use an app on the phone for this? Might try one soon.

confounders.alternative_explanation: Starting a new job three weeks ago and feeling under pressure could explain the slips.
confounders.quote: some of this is just that it's new and I'm trying hard not to get things wrong

design.knowledge_target: Weighing a help-seeking message: over-explaining or minimising style, borrowed opinions of others, and what the text cannot show (onset, breadth, impairment).

planted_cues.quote: it sat open on my screen until the next afternoon before I sent it
walked into the stock room and forgotten what I went in for

design.purpose: asking for an appointment because things at work keep slipping (traits: task_initiation: moderate; working_memory: weak)

vignettes.text: Hello, I'm very sorry to trouble you, and I hope this is the right way to ask for an appointment. I'm 27 and have been registered with you since university, though I've only been in twice. Three weeks ago I started my first job, at a logistics firm, and honestly I think some of this is just that it's new and I'm trying hard not to get things wrong. The first week was fine. I was early every day and finished my induction modules by the Friday, which I was pleased about. Since then a few things have slipped. Last Tuesday my manager asked me to send a supplier a corrected spreadsheet, and I knew exactly what to do, but it sat open on my screen until the next afternoon before I sent it. Twice I've walked into the stock room and forgotten what I went in for, which I know is small. My manager has been kind about it, and the planner I bought last week has helped with remembering meetings. I'm sorry this is so long. Could I please have an appointment, either early morning or after 5pm, as I would rather not explain to work yet?

confounders.alternative_explanation: Typing in a hurry on a phone after a night shift explains the typos and the scattered, fragmentary style.
confounders.quote: Typing this on my phone with useless thumbs after twelve hours so excuse the typos.

design.knowledge_target: Separating fragmentation caused by medium, haste or fatigue from fragmentation that reflects attentional lapses (self-interruption mid-clause, lost referents).

planted_cues.quote: ended up restocking glove boxes down the whole corridor, remembered the chart at 5
wrote it on my hand because the list is in my locker. or my coat.

design.purpose: a note about the week, typed between tasks (traits: distractibility: moderate; working_memory: moderate)

vignettes.text: Wed. 6:50, bus in ten. Week so far. Mon was quiet apart from bed 14 who coded at 3, we got him back, handover done by 7 with nothing missed. Tue the pharmcy delivery came late so I spent an hour chasing saline stock, not my fault for once. Went to do the fluid balance on bed 9 and ended up restocking glove boxes down the whole corridor, remembered the chart at 5. Done before handover anyway. Last night Dana covered my break and I sat down for the full 30 min, ate the rice thing. Nothing happened. Need to ask about swapping the Sunday, wrote it on my hand because the list is in my locker. or my coat. Typing this on my phone with useless thumbs after twelve hours so excuse the typos. Bus. Also milk.

confounders.alternative_explanation: Low mood for several weeks after a break-up could account for the irritability and the sharp outburst.
confounders.quote: I've felt flat since the break-up, about five weeks now

design.knowledge_target: Reading emotional reactivity in text: fast tone shifts with fast recovery versus persistent low mood, and what a single entry cannot show.

planted_cues.quote: loud enough for two customers, that it was the third time and did anyone here actually read the planogram
I started pulling the signs down myself before she'd even answered.

design.purpose: snapping at a colleague and then feeling awful about it (traits: emotional_reactivity: moderate; quick_to_act: weak)

vignettes.text: Snapped at Priya today. Not proud. She'd put the spring display up on the wrong wall and I said, loud enough for two customers, that it was the third time and did anyone here actually read the planogram. I started pulling the signs down myself before she'd even answered. Then she went quiet and I went to the stockroom and counted boxes I'd already counted. Sorry. Genuinely. She'd been in since six and covered for Tomas, so the wall thing was a bad call on my side too, I never told her which wall. I should have just said that. Rest of the day was fine. Delivery arrived on time, till float matched to the penny, and the Friday rota went out before lunch like I'd planned. I stayed calm with the man who wanted a refund without a receipt, which I'm weirdly happy about. I've felt flat since the break-up, about five weeks now, so maybe that's some of it. Maybe not. Don't want to use it as an excuse. Bought her a coffee at four. She said it was fine. I don't think it was. Will say it properly tomorrow before opening, or text tonight. Not sure. Text, probably.

confounders.alternative_explanation: Many of the childhood memories are second-hand, retold by the parents, so they may be embellished or reflect the parents' framing rather than the writer's own recall.
confounders.quote: I don't actually remember that, it's one of her stories

design.knowledge_target: Weighing retrospective childhood accounts in text (specific episodes versus generic labels, second-hand memories) for the childhood-onset requirement.

planted_cues.quote: sit at the kitchen table with the maths sheet for most of the evening, pencil sharpened twice, before I wrote a single number
walking home the long way and arriving an hour late because I was watching the men dig up the road

design.purpose: remembering how school went and what the teachers wrote on report cards (traits: task_initiation: moderate; distractibility: moderate, recalled from childhood)

vignettes.text: So I was going through the box Mum sent and found my year four report. Mrs Okafor wrote that I was capable, polite and a strong reader, which is nice to see in her handwriting. Mum says I would sit at the kitchen table with the maths sheet for most of the evening, pencil sharpened twice, before I wrote a single number. I don't actually remember that, it's one of her stories, same as the one about me walking home the long way and arriving an hour late because I was watching the men dig up the road. Dad tells that one every Christmas. What I do remember myself is the science fair, year six or seven, I'm hazy. I planned the volcano the week before, bought the baking soda on the Tuesday and had it finished early. It got a ribbon. Mr Doyle wrote that I was a pleasure to teach when I knew what was expected. The handwriting comment came every year though, untidy and rushed. You got the neat ones. I'd love to see yours if Mum kept them, she said the loft, or maybe the garage.

confounders.alternative_explanation: The writer is naturally talkative and enjoys telling stories at length.
confounders.quote: you know I never tell a short version

confounders.alternative_explanation: Talkativeness is an ordinary personality trait of someone who enjoys storytelling.
confounders.quote: I talked the whole way back

design.knowledge_target: Hard negative: long, digressive but organised storytelling that must not be read as attentional (style versus trait).
design.purpose: telling a neighbour about a fishing trip last summer (control: none: this person has no notable attention or organisation difficulties)

vignettes.text: Hello Frank, you asked how the fishing trip went, so here it is, and you know I never tell a short version. We left Harlow at five on the Saturday, which I had planned for a week, and we reached the lake by quarter to seven. Dennis drove because my knee was sore, and after thirty-one years behind the wheel of a bus it feels odd to sit in the passenger seat. Anyway. We hired the little boat from the man at the jetty, the same man as last year, and he remembered my name, which pleased me. I caught a perch first and then nothing for two hours. Dennis caught three roach and mentioned it often. Margaret made the sandwiches, ham and mustard, and they lasted until about noon. The maggots Dennis brought were the wrong kind for roach, so the jetty man sold us a tub of worms and that sorted it. Around three the wind got up and we came in early. The roads were clear and we were home by six. I talked the whole way back, Dennis says, though I don't remember much of it. Come round Thursday and I'll show you the photos. There are eleven, or twelve, I'd have to count.
